lesson.title: A Government Too Weak to Govern
lesson.summary: The Articles of Confederation, the nation's first constitution, created a deliberately weak central government that could win independence but could not manage the peace that followed.
lesson.body:
After the Second Continental Congress had spent years coordinating the war effort without any formal constitutional basis for doing so, delegates recognized the new nation needed some written framework for national government. The Articles of Confederation were drafted starting in 1776, adopted by Congress in November 1777, and finally ratified by all thirteen states on March 1, 1781, after Maryland held out for years over unresolved disputes about western land claims held by other states.

The document that emerged reflected deep American suspicion of centralized power, a suspicion earned through years of resenting a distant king and Parliament. The Articles created what they themselves called a firm league of friendship among sovereign states rather than a true national government. There was no president, no national court system, and no power for Congress to tax citizens directly. Each state, regardless of size, got exactly one vote, and passing any significant legislation required agreement from nine of the thirteen states. Amending the Articles at all required the unanimous consent of every state, a bar so high it was never once cleared.

This was not simply bad design. It was the design many Americans wanted. Memories of British taxation and a distant, unaccountable executive were fresh, and state legislatures were reluctant to hand power to a national body that might replicate those abuses. Congress under the Articles had no separate executive branch and no national court system at all, so whatever limited business it conducted, including trying to make good on the terms of the Treaty of Paris, had to be handled by committees of the same single legislative body.

The Articles did produce real achievements, most notably the Northwest Ordinance of 1787, which organized the territory north of the Ohio River, banned slavery there, and laid out an orderly process for new territories to eventually join the union as equal states rather than remaining permanent colonies of the original thirteen.

But the weaknesses proved crippling once the immediate emergency of war had passed. Congress could ask states for money to pay Revolutionary War debts but could not force them to pay, leaving the treasury chronically empty. It had no power to regulate trade between states or with foreign nations, so states taxed each other's goods and undercut one another in negotiations with foreign powers. And as seen with the Treaty of Paris, Congress could sign international agreements but had no reliable way to make states or citizens honor them.

By the mid 1780s, this weakness was no longer an abstract problem for political theorists to argue about. It was showing up as unpaid soldiers, worthless currency, and squabbling states, setting the stage for the crisis that would soon erupt in the Massachusetts countryside and force American leaders to reconsider the entire structure of their government.
